meta.name: AWS Certified Database Specialty (DBS-C01)
meta.notes: [scheduled-agent initial authoring 2026-07-15: 12 exam-style questions across the five DBS-C01 domains — workload-specific database design, deployment and migration, management and operations, monitoring and troubleshooting, database security; balanced correct-answer distribution 3/3/3/3; length-matched distractors] [hardening pass 2026-08-13: re-shuffled all 12 correct positions (3/3/3/3 preserved), tightened option-length parity across all questions, rewrote distractors so each names a real AWS feature with a specific-but-wrong mechanism, expanded every explanation to state why each distractor is wrong, removed stem-word echoes from correct-option descriptors]

questions.question: A gaming company stores real-time leaderboards for 40 million players. Each write updates a single player's score and each read fetches the top 100 scores for a game session. The workload sees single-digit-millisecond latency requirements at 250,000 requests per second with unpredictable spikes. Which database service best fits these requirements?
options: Aurora PostgreSQL with a materialized view of the top scores refreshed every 5 seconds by a scheduled Lambda function
Amazon RDS for MySQL with a read replica per Region and application-side sharding by player_id ranges across shards
Amazon DocumentDB with a compound index on game_id and score, backed by an in-cluster cache warm-up worker fleet
Amazon MemoryDB for Redis using sorted sets (ZADD/ZRANGE) with Multi-AZ replication for durable primary storage
questions.explanation: MemoryDB for Redis provides in-memory single-digit-millisecond performance and native sorted-set commands (ZADD/ZRANGE) that model leaderboards as a ranked structure, and its Multi-AZ transaction log gives it the durability of a primary datastore rather than only a cache. Aurora PostgreSQL with a materialized view cannot refresh often enough to serve real-time top-N under 250k RPS and adds relational planning overhead. RDS for MySQL with application-side sharding pushes correctness burden into the app and still cannot meet the latency ceiling under spikes because each shard is a single writer. DocumentDB is a JSON document store with no native ranked-set primitive — a top-N query becomes a scan of a secondary index that keeps growing.

questions.question: A company runs a self-managed PostgreSQL 14 database on EC2 that is 3.2 TB in size and cannot tolerate more than 5 minutes of downtime during the migration to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The source has heavy ongoing write activity. Which migration approach minimizes downtime?
options: Take a pg_dump of the source, restore it into Aurora with pg_restore, and repoint the application after the restore has finished
Create the Aurora cluster from a manual EBS snapshot of the EC2 instance's data volume and start the cluster from that snapshot
Use AWS DMS with a full-load-plus-CDC task from the EC2 PostgreSQL instance to Aurora, then cut over after CDC lag drains to zero
Enable native logical replication from the source to Aurora using pglogical, without AWS DMS, and cut over once replicas are caught up
questions.explanation: AWS DMS with a full-load-plus-CDC task snapshots the source and then continuously applies changes captured from the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, so cutover only requires stopping writes long enough for the last few CDC events to drain — well under 5 minutes for a healthy pipeline. pg_dump/pg_restore requires a write freeze for the entire dump-and-restore window, which for 3.2 TB is hours. Aurora cannot be built from an EBS snapshot of a self-managed instance — the Aurora storage engine only imports from RDS snapshots or from S3 dumps of supported formats. Native pglogical works but is operationally heavier than DMS, provides no downtime advantage that DMS+CDC doesn't already offer, and needs superuser-level setup on the source.

questions.question: An Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster serves an application that opens and closes short-lived database connections for every HTTP request from a fleet of AWS Lambda functions. During traffic spikes the writer instance runs out of max_connections and the application sees frequent connection errors. What is the MOST effective remediation?
options: Increase the writer instance size until max_connections is high enough to accept every concurrent Lambda invocation directly
Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the cluster and have the Lambda functions connect through the proxy's endpoint hostname
Move the workload to Aurora Serverless v2 so the connection pool is managed automatically as capacity units scale
Enable the Aurora cluster endpoint's failover feature to distribute Lambda connections across the reader replicas in the cluster
questions.explanation: RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections between many application clients (like a Lambda fleet) and a limited number of backend connections, which is the standard fix for connection exhaustion caused by short-lived, high-churn clients. Sizing up the writer buys headroom on max_connections but does not solve the underlying connection churn and gets expensive quickly. Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute but does not manage the connection pool for you — a huge Lambda fleet still opens and closes physical connections just as fast and exhausts backend slots. The cluster endpoint always points at the writer and does no client load balancing; only the reader endpoint round-robins across replicas, and reader endpoints cannot serve writes anyway.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table stores IoT sensor readings with partition key device_id and sort key event_ts. A query for the last 24 hours of readings for a single device returns quickly, but a query that filters events across ALL devices for a given tenant_id runs a full scan and is far too slow. What is the LEAST expensive way to accelerate the tenant query without changing the base table schema?
options: Create a global secondary index (GSI) with tenant_id as the partition key and event_ts as the sort key and query the GSI
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table so the scan hits the DAX cluster's cache instead of the table itself
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so the scan can burst without provisioned throughput throttling on the base table
Add a local secondary index (LSI) on tenant_id and issue a Query operation for the tenant instead of the current Scan operation
questions.explanation: A GSI lets you query DynamoDB by an attribute that is not the base table's partition key without touching the base schema. A GSI with tenant_id as the partition key and event_ts as the sort key turns the tenant query into an efficient Query (log-N) instead of a Scan (O-N). DAX caches Query and GetItem responses but has no scan-caching semantics that meaningfully help a full-table Scan, and each miss still pays the full Scan cost. On-demand capacity removes provisioned-throughput throttling but does not reduce the amount of data scanned or its dollar cost — you still pay per RCU read. LSIs must share the base partition key (device_id) and can only be created at table-creation time, so an LSI on tenant_id is not even valid here.

questions.question: A fintech customer must retain 7 years of point-in-time backups for a production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database to satisfy an auditor. Automated backups on RDS retain only up to 35 days. What is the recommended way to meet the 7-year retention requirement with the LEAST operational effort?
options: Take a manual RDS snapshot every day with an EventBridge rule and delete snapshots older than 2555 days with a scheduled Lambda job
Enable cross-Region automated backup replication to a secondary Region and rely on that Region's 35-day retention window for long-term storage
Turn on continuous export of the transaction logs to Amazon S3 with a Lifecycle policy that transitions objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days
Register the RDS instance with AWS Backup and use a backup plan whose lifecycle rules transition to cold storage and expire after 7 years
questions.explanation: AWS Backup centrally manages RDS backups with backup plans that support cold-storage transitions and expiration measured in years — exactly the long-retention use case, with the least operational effort because AWS runs the scheduling, retention, and lifecycle machinery for you. Rolling your own EventBridge + Lambda snapshot pipeline works but re-implements what AWS Backup already provides and adds code you have to own. Cross-Region automated backup replication is a disaster-recovery feature — the destination Region's retention is still bounded by the source's automated-backup window (max 35 days), so it does not extend total retention. RDS does not support continuous transaction-log export to S3 as a first-class feature (only automated snapshots and PITR within the retention window), so that option is fabricated.

questions.question: A social-graph application stores users, their friends, and the friend-of-friend relationships. The most common queries are "find all friends within 3 hops of user X who live in the same city" and "suggest new friends based on shared interests." Query latency must stay under 100 ms even at billions of edges. Which database service best fits this workload?
options: Amazon DynamoDB with an adjacency-list pattern and a GSI per relationship direction to store and traverse the friend edges
Amazon Neptune with the Gremlin query language and a property graph model that stores users and friend edges natively
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with recursive Common Table Expressions over a friends table indexed on both endpoint columns
Amazon DocumentDB with a nested-array friends field and a per-interest secondary index driving application-side traversal
questions.explanation: Neptune is a purpose-built graph database whose query engines (Gremlin, openCypher, SPARQL) traverse multi-hop relationships in near-constant time relative to the number of touched edges, which is exactly what "friends within N hops" needs at scale. DynamoDB adjacency lists can model graphs, but multi-hop traversals require one round-trip per hop and quickly blow past 100 ms once each hop's fan-out is large. Recursive CTEs on Aurora work at small scale but degrade sharply on billions of edges because the planner materialises the whole traversal set. DocumentDB stores nested arrays but has no graph-traversal engine — you end up doing the traversal in application code, which is neither fast nor bounded.

questions.question: An Aurora MySQL cluster's writer instance recently failed over to a reader. The failover took approximately 90 seconds — much longer than the expected 30-second window. The DBA reviews Performance Insights and finds a single long-running transaction that had been open for 40 minutes at the time of failover. What is the MOST likely cause of the extended failover time?
options: The promoted reader had to roll back the long-running open transaction before accepting writes, which extended the failover window
The Aurora cluster endpoint DNS TTL was not honored by the client, so the client kept connecting to the failed writer for over a minute
The reader replica was in a different Availability Zone and cross-AZ promotion always adds significant time on Aurora MySQL clusters
The cluster had only one reader, and Aurora had to provision a new writer instance from the shared storage volume during the failover
questions.explanation: When a reader is promoted to writer, it must first roll back any in-flight transactions from the old writer before it can safely accept new writes; a 40-minute open transaction produces a large undo pile that takes considerable time to unwind, which is the classic cause of unexpectedly long Aurora failovers. Cross-AZ promotion adds only a few seconds on Aurora because storage is shared across AZs and no data has to be re-shipped. Client-side DNS caching lengthens the client's perception of failover but not the cluster-reported failover duration (which is what the 90 s figure measures). Aurora does not "provision a new writer instance from storage" during a normal failover — it promotes an existing reader; the scenario states a reader was promoted, so that option contradicts the facts.

questions.question: A regulated healthcare application requires that ALL database credentials used by application servers be rotated automatically every 30 days without downtime, and that no static credentials appear in application configuration or environment variables. The database is Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST custom code?
options: Store the database password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a SecureString and rewrite the value every 30 days with a scheduled Lambda
Store the credentials in an encrypted S3 object with a Lifecycle policy that expires the object every 30 days, forcing the operator to upload a fresh copy
Store the database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation on a 30-day schedule and let the app fetch them via the Secrets Manager SDK
Enable RDS Proxy with IAM authentication and let the proxy issue short-lived tokens; keep a long-lived master password in a KMS-encrypted file on the app servers
questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager natively supports automatic rotation of RDS credentials using Lambda rotation templates that AWS publishes — no custom code and no application downtime because the rotation strategy alternates between two active credential versions on the database. Parameter Store SecureString can hold a password but has no built-in RDS rotation, so the Lambda would be entirely custom. An encrypted S3 object with a Lifecycle expiry is not credential rotation at all — expiring an object just deletes it. RDS Proxy with IAM auth eliminates application-side passwords in principle, but the described design still stores a long-lived master password on the app servers, which directly violates the "no static credentials in configuration" requirement.

questions.question: An Amazon RDS for SQL Server instance is showing high CPU utilization during business hours. The DBA needs to identify which specific SQL statements and wait events are consuming the most database time over the last 7 days, correlated with load. Which native AWS feature provides this analysis with the LEAST setup?
options: Turn on Enhanced Monitoring at 1-second granularity and analyze the process-level CPU counters that surface in CloudWatch Logs metrics
Export the SQL Server error log to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and run Logs Insights queries to aggregate query durations across the window
Attach the SQL Server sys.dm_os_wait_stats DMV output to a self-managed Grafana dashboard fed by a Lambda that polls the instance every minute
Enable Amazon RDS Performance Insights on the instance and use the dashboard's Top SQL and Top Wait Events views over a 7-day window
questions.explanation: Performance Insights is the AWS-native tool for exactly this: it captures DB load broken down by SQL statement and by wait event on a rolling multi-day retention (7 days free, up to 2 years paid) with no code changes and no on-instance agents. Enhanced Monitoring shows OS-level metrics (per-process CPU, memory, disk) but not SQL text or database wait breakdowns, so it cannot identify the offending statements. The SQL Server error log does not record query execution stats — only server events and errors — so aggregating durations from it is not possible. Rolling a Grafana pipeline over DMVs is technically possible but has by far the most setup and does not correlate load the way Performance Insights already does out of the box.

questions.question: An organization runs a mission-critical Aurora PostgreSQL cluster in eu-west-1. Regulatory requirements demand that a fully functional read/write replica be available in us-east-1 within 1 minute of an eu-west-1 Regional outage, with an RPO of under 1 second. Which architecture meets these requirements?
options: An Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in us-east-1 and managed planned failover configured for cross-Region promotion
A cross-Region Aurora read replica created from the eu-west-1 writer, promoted to a standalone cluster during failover using a manual API call
Cross-Region automated backup replication with a Lambda that provisions a fresh Aurora cluster in us-east-1 from the latest snapshot during an outage
A pair of Aurora clusters kept in sync via AWS DMS full-load-plus-CDC in both directions, with Route 53 health-check-based failover between them
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database is purpose-built for this: it replicates from the primary Region to secondary Regions via dedicated storage-layer replication with typical lag under 1 second (RPO), and managed planned failover promotes a secondary cluster to primary in well under a minute (RTO). A cross-Region Aurora read replica has higher lag (measured in seconds to minutes) and manual promotion is slower and requires more human steps. Rebuilding from cross-Region snapshots is a DR pattern with an RTO of many minutes to hours and an RPO of at least the snapshot cadence. Bidirectional DMS pipelines cannot guarantee sub-second RPO, do not natively resolve write conflicts, and add operational risk that violates the mission-critical requirement.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table backing an e-commerce cart is provisioned with 4,000 write capacity units. One partition key value — the flagship product's cart_id — receives 60% of all writes during a flash sale, causing hot-partition throttling even though average utilization is well below capacity. What is the MOST effective schema change to eliminate the hot partition?
options: Switch the table from provisioned to on-demand capacity mode so per-partition throttling no longer applies during traffic spikes and bursts
Introduce write sharding by appending a random suffix (0..N) to the flagship cart_id so writes fan out across N logical partition keys
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table so hot-key writes are absorbed by the DAX write-through cache before hitting the base table
Add a global secondary index on the cart_id attribute so writes to the flagship key are automatically spread across the GSI's own partitions
questions.explanation: Write sharding — appending a random suffix like cart_id#0..N to the hot key so writes distribute across N logical partitions — is the canonical DynamoDB pattern for eliminating hot partitions caused by a single dominant key, and the reader recombines shards on read. On-demand capacity still enforces the per-partition-throughput ceiling (roughly 1,000 WCU per partition), so a single hot key can still throttle even in on-demand mode. DAX is a read-through cache; writes are pass-through and inherit the base table's per-partition limits, so it does not shield writes at all. A GSI does not spread writes on the same key across more partitions of the base table — it just projects those writes into another index that would need its own partition-key change, so on its own it is not a fix.

questions.question: A compliance policy requires that any RDS snapshot shared with another AWS account, or copied to another Region, remains encrypted end-to-end with a customer-managed KMS key that never leaves the source account's control. Which approach satisfies the policy?
options: Encrypt the snapshot with the default aws/rds AWS-managed key and share it directly with the destination account, which will decrypt it on import
Copy the snapshot to the destination Region unencrypted first, then re-encrypt it in the destination Region with a new customer-managed KMS key
Encrypt the snapshot with a customer-managed KMS key, grant the destination account kms:CreateGrant on that key, and share the snapshot
Export the snapshot to Amazon S3 with server-side encryption using SSE-S3 and grant the destination account cross-account access to the S3 bucket
questions.explanation: RDS supports sharing encrypted snapshots across accounts only when the snapshot is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key (not the AWS-managed aws/rds key) and the destination account is granted access via a KMS grant (kms:CreateGrant) on that key — this keeps key control in the source account while allowing the destination to decrypt through the grant. The AWS-managed aws/rds key cannot be shared across accounts and cannot back a cross-account snapshot share at all. Copying unencrypted first violates the end-to-end encryption requirement, and RDS refuses to produce an unencrypted copy of an encrypted snapshot anyway. Exporting to S3 with SSE-S3 replaces KMS with S3-managed keys, which removes customer control over the key material and breaks the policy.
